thesis: The Thema 8.32 really did run a Ferrari-cast V8 -- cast at Maranello itself -- but Lancia and Ducati deliberately reengineered it (a different crankshaft, smaller valves, a different firing order) specifically so it would NOT feel like a Ferrari, trading race-bred character for saloon-car smoothness. That's more interesting, and more precise, than either 'just a Ferrari engine' or the vaguer 'Ferrari-derived' usually gets credit for -- and it's part of why a car that cost roughly triple a standard Thema, in a run of under four thousand, stayed a footnote rather than becoming a cult icon.
hook: In the mid-1980s, Lancia put a genuine Ferrari-cast V8 -- cast at Maranello itself -- into a plain three-box executive sedan, then had it deliberately reengineered so it wouldn't feel like a Ferrari at all.
runtime_rationale: 10 minutes, near the low end of the channel's normal_range_minutes, below the 12-minute preferred_minutes center. This episode's evidence is real but thinner than the channel's Cimarron pilot: no primary document equivalent to a manufacturer brochure, several claims single-sourced (perf01, price01, eq01, own02), one important thread -- who actually originated the project -- left as two unreconciled competing attributions (dev01/dev02) rather than a clean story, and one contemporary source (rec02, Quattroruote) found but unreadable. Beats covering unresolved/hedged material run shorter, not longer, than a fully-evidenced beat would -- hedging compresses screen time rather than filling it. Six beats of moderate density land naturally under 12 minutes without padding.
open_questions: dev01 vs dev02: two sources name two different people (Andre Chardonnet, a French importer, vs Vittorio Ghidella, Fiat's CEO) as the originator of the Ferrari-engine idea, with no source reconciling them. A French-language follow-up pass (fr.wikipedia.org's Chardonnet biography, or opening guideautoweb.com/caradisiac.com directly rather than via search synthesis) is the most promising next step.

price01 (UK 1988 price, £37,500) is single-sourced and is specifically a UK market figure for a left-hand-drive-only car (own02) -- no original Italian domestic launch price was found. Worth finding a period Italian price to know whether the UK figure reflects import premium or the car's actual list price.

rec02 confirms a June 1987 Quattroruote road test exists but its content (positive/negative, specific findings) is unknown -- this environment can't process video. If the episode wants genuine contemporary Italian critical reaction (as opposed to the English-language retrospective in rec01), transcribing or finding a text version of that test is the way to get it.

beats.purpose: Open on the central tension -- a plain sedan hiding a genuinely Ferrari-cast engine -- and set up the question the episode answers: how Ferrari is it, really?
beats.summary: A conventional-looking three-box Italian executive sedan from the mid-1980s concealed a 2.9-litre V8 cast at Ferrari's own Maranello plant -- 215 PS in its uncatalyzed form, enough for 0-100 km/h in under seven seconds.
beats.narration_direction: Lead with the visual mismatch (plain sedan / Ferrari-cast engine) before naming the car. eng01 supports 'genuinely Ferrari-cast' plainly. Performance figures (eng04, perf01) are safe but perf01 is single-sourced -- keep it as color, not a headline claim. Do not resolve the 'how Ferrari is it' question yet -- that's b3.

visual_requests.description: Exterior shot emphasizing the conventional three-box saloon look, ideally without the 8.32 badge legible yet.

visual_requests.subject: Thema 8.32 V8 engine bay
visual_requests.description: Engine bay shot of the transverse-mounted Ferrari V8.

beats.purpose: Show how the project began -- and be honest that the record itself is unresolved about whose idea it was.
beats.summary: Two competing accounts exist for who proposed fitting a Ferrari V8 to the Thema: French-language sources credit Andre Chardonnet, Lancia's independent French importer; an English-language feature instead credits Fiat Group CEO Vittorio Ghidella with championing the project and building its production line. Neither source cites evidence for its claim, and nothing reconciles the two.
beats.narration_direction: Present both attributions explicitly as competing accounts rather than picking one -- this beat's honesty about not knowing is more interesting than a false clean origin story would be. Both claims are individually medium-confidence and airable, but the SYNTHESIS ('here's definitively who did it') is not supported by either alone.

visual_requests.subject: Vittorio Ghidella and/or Andre Chardonnet, mid-1980s
visual_requests.description: Period photo of either named individual if available.

visual_requests.subject: 1986 Turin Motor Show
visual_requests.description: Footage/photos of the Turin show where the 8.32 was unveiled; period-appropriate substitutes acceptable.

beats.purpose: Deliver the thesis: a real Ferrari engine, deliberately made to not feel like one.
beats.summary: Ferrari cast the block at Maranello; Ducati assembled it; Lancia's Turin plant built it into the car. But the crankshaft was swapped from the flat-plane type used in contemporary Ferrari road cars to a cross-plane design, the valves were made smaller, and the firing order was changed -- all specifically so the engine would deliver smooth saloon-car torque rather than a sports car's high-revving snarl.
beats.narration_direction: This is the core beat -- state plainly that this WAS a genuine Ferrari engine (eng01/eng03) and then pivot to exactly what was changed and why (eng02). Avoid both oversimplifications the fact pack flags: don't say 'it wasn't really a Ferrari engine', and don't stop at 'Ferrari engine' without the modification.

visual_requests.subject: Ferrari 308/Mondial Quattrovalvole V8 vs Thema 8.32 V8
visual_requests.description: Side-by-side or comparison graphic of the donor Ferrari engine and the modified Thema unit, ideally highlighting the crankshaft difference.

visual_requests.subject: Maranello casting / Ducati assembly of the era
visual_requests.description: Period manufacturing imagery; generic Ferrari-era Maranello or Ducati factory material acceptable if the specific process isn't available.

beats.purpose: Ground the engineering story in what a buyer actually got and paid.
beats.summary: Standard equipment included a driver-controlled retractable rear spoiler, ABS, power steering, and a wood-and-Alcantara interior, offered with a 5-speed manual only -- no automatic was ever built. In the UK in 1988 it listed at £37,500, roughly triple the £12,495 asked for a base Thema in the same market that year.
beats.narration_direction: Use d02's safe_wording for the price comparison -- 'roughly three times', with the UK/1988/base-Thema comparator stated, never an unqualified 'it cost 3x a Thema'. price01 is single-sourced and UK-specific -- flag this is a British price for a left-hand-drive-only car, not confirmed as the original Italian price.

visual_requests.subject: Thema 8.32 interior
visual_requests.description: Interior shot showing the wood-and-Alcantara trim and retractable rear spoiler control.

visual_requests.subject: 1988 UK price list or period advertisement
visual_requests.description: Period pricing document if one survives, to support the £37,500 figure on screen.

beats.purpose: Show what contemporary and retrospective press actually said, honestly marking what could and couldn't be verified.
beats.summary: A contemporary road test ran in Italy's Quattroruote magazine in June 1987, though its content isn't available here to characterize. Road & Track's own later retrospective called the car 'one of the weirder sleepers to come out of the 1980s' -- a judgment made well after launch, not at the time.
beats.narration_direction: rec02 may only be used to note that a contemporary Italian test existed and when -- never to characterize what it concluded. rec01's quote is explicitly retrospective (per its own 'out of the 1980s' framing) -- do not present it as a period reaction.

visual_requests.subject: June 1987 Quattroruote issue/cover
visual_requests.description: Cover or masthead of the June 1987 Quattroruote issue containing the road test, to support the existence claim on screen without needing its content.

beats.purpose: Close on scale and a memorable ownership detail, landing the thesis's 'stayed a footnote' claim.
beats.summary: Total production across both series was 3,971 cars -- 2,370 first-series examples from 1986-1988, 1,601 second-series cars taking the run to 1992 -- all left-hand drive only. Enzo Ferrari himself reportedly kept one as his personal car in his final years.
beats.narration_direction: Production numbers are the pack's best-corroborated statistics (three independent sources, arithmetic checked via d01) -- state them plainly. Close on own01 with its 'reportedly' hedge intact per its safe_wording; it's a strong closing image precisely because the man whose company's name was on the castings chose to drive one.

visual_requests.description: A Series 2 car for visual variety/closure.

visual_requests.description: A period photo of Enzo Ferrari from the mid-to-late 1980s; does not need to show him with the car specifically.
